title: Two Simple Questions to Help Students Improve Performance in Your Current Unit ent-unit
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart offers a compact, replicable protocol for deepening unit understanding in any subject in just 5-10 minutes: identify two key concepts from the current unit, have students write how the concepts are similar and different, then discuss as a class while pushing for precision. He gives concrete examples across disciplines — maritime versus land-based empires in world history, similes versus metaphors in literature, log versus exponential statements in pre-calc — to show the technique's range. The pedagogical justification is elaboration, the cognitive-science principle that thinking about the meaning and relationships within to-be-learned material improves retention, which Stuart traces back to research from 1975 and later studies showing students can be explicitly taught to elaborate. The piece functions as a low-cost, high-leverage classroom routine that Stuart frames as usable "tomorrow," independent of whether readers are interested in his forthcoming course.
points: The protocol is deliberately minimal — one pair of concepts, two comparison questions, 5-10 minutes — designed to be usable the next day without any planning overhead, regardless of subject area.
Cross-discipline examples (empires in history, literary devices in English, logs versus exponentials in math) demonstrate that comparing key concepts is a content-agnostic elaboration technique.
The technique is grounded in decades-old cognitive-science research (dating to 1975) on elaboration and depth of processing, distinguishing it from a merely intuitive classroom trick.
Stuart's instruction to "let them struggle a bit" while circulating signals that some productive difficulty is a feature of the task, not something to preempt by over-scaffolding.
quotes: Is it possible to help your students significantly deepen their understanding of your current unit, regardless of content area? Yes. And it need only take 5-10 minutes of class time.
First, identify a handful of concepts that are especially important for the unit your students are working on.
As the students wrestle with your questions, walk around. Look at what they are doing on the page. Ask them about where they are struggling. Do let them struggle a bit.
When you ask students to think about the relationships between key concepts in your course, you're asking them to do what cognitive scientists call elaboration.

Going back as far as 1975, researchers have been demonstrating that when students think about the meaning of what they are tasked with learning, their ability to retain and use what they've learned increases.

Ultimately, we want to teach our students how to do this kind of elaboration themselves. This is what researchers did in another study where learners were taught elaboration techniques and then performed better on subsequent tests of memory.
Whether the course interests you are not, try asking your students to compare 2-3 key concepts tomorrow. Let me know how it goes.
